# Software Implementation {.unnumbered}
 
Now that our hardware is wired for deep sleep, we need to restructure the firmware.

When the RTC alarm wakes the ESP32 up, it doesn't resume where it left off: it restarts from the beginning of `setup()`.

Therefore, in this deep-sleep design, **we do not use the `loop()` function at all**. All the logic (reading sensors, saving to SD, setting the next alarm, and going back to sleep) runs sequentially inside `setup()`.

## The Code

> **Further Reading:** The alarm logic used in this phase is adapted from the official [Adafruit RTClib DS3231_alarm example](https://github.com/adafruit/RTClib/blob/master/examples/DS3231_alarm/DS3231_alarm.ino). The [EOLab Deep Sleep Wiki](https://wiki.eolab.de/doku.php?id=amc2020:group_n:deepsleep) covers the same DS3231 + ESP32 setup in more depth.
>
> *(Note on the pull-up resistor: EOLab uses a 100kΩ pull-up on `SQW` to minimize the current drawn while the alarm is active. We use 10kΩ, which draws a bit more during the few milliseconds the alarm is active, but gives a stiffer, less noise-sensitive signal. Both work.)*

> **Ready-to-use project:** The complete code for this power management phase is available in the repository here: [`05_power_management_rtc`](https://github.com/wg1d/personal-autonomous-weather-station/tree/main/firmware/PoC/Phase-02/05_power_management_rtc)


## How It Works

1.  **Print Wake-up Reason:** The helper function `print_wakeup_reason()` shows what triggered the boot: our RTC alarm (`EXT0`) or a standard power-on.
2.  **Conditional Time Setting (`lostPower`):** We do *not* set the time unconditionally with `rtc.adjust()`: it would reset the clock to the compile time at every wake-up. The time is only set if the RTC reports a power loss (first use, or coin cell removed or depleted). As in Phase 01, the compile time is converted to UTC.
3.  **RTC Configuration:** We disable the 32 kHz output (`rtc.disable32K()`), which also saves a little power, switch the SQW pin to interrupt mode (`rtc.writeSqwPinMode(DS3231_OFF)`), and disable the unused Alarm 2 (`rtc.disableAlarm(2)`).
4.  **Clear Alarms:** When an alarm triggers, the DS3231 sets an alarm flag and pulls SQW LOW. This flag is *latched*: SQW stays LOW until the flag is cleared over I2C. `rtc.clearAlarm(1)` and `rtc.clearAlarm(2)` release the SQW line, so that it goes back HIGH and can signal the next alarm.
5.  **BME280 in Forced Mode:** By default, the Adafruit library configures the BME280 in *normal mode*: the sensor measures continuously, and it keeps doing so while the ESP32 sleeps, since it is still powered. This wastes several hundred µA (see the [power budget](02-hardware-modifications.qmd#power-budget-estimates)) and slightly heats the sensor, which biases the temperature. We switch it to **forced mode** with `setSampling()`: `takeForcedMeasurement()` triggers a single measurement, after which the sensor automatically returns to sleep. The settings we use (1x oversampling, no filter) are the ones recommended by Bosch for weather monitoring.
6.  **Sequential Execution:** We read the sensor, turn on the SD card using `SD_OFF_PIN`, save the data with `now.toString()` for the timestamp, unmount the card with `SD.end()`, and turn it back off.
7.  **Set the Next Alarm (Grid Snapping):** We compute the next alarm on a fixed grid: `next = now - (now % interval) + interval`. The modulo `now % interval` is the time elapsed since the last grid slot: subtracting it brings us back to that slot, and adding `interval` gives the next one. For example, with a 30-second interval, a wake-up at `16:00:17` gives `17 % 30 = 17` (in seconds), so `next = 16:00:17 - 17 s + 30 s = 16:00:30`. The station therefore wakes up at `16:00:00`, `16:00:30`, `16:01:00`, and so on. If a wake-up happens off-grid (after a reset, or a manual wake-up in Phase 3), the next one automatically realigns on the grid.
    *   We read the time **again** right before computing the alarm, instead of reusing the timestamp read at wake-up. If the work done during the wake-up (SD card, and later Wi-Fi) takes longer than the interval, an alarm computed from the wake-up time would already be in the past. Because the alarm matches hours, minutes and seconds (see below), it would then only fire **the next day**.
    *   *The `DS3231_A1_Second` Gotcha:* The official [Adafruit RTClib DS3231_alarm example](https://github.com/adafruit/RTClib/blob/master/examples/DS3231_alarm/DS3231_alarm.ino) uses the `DS3231_A1_Second` flag, which means **"match only the seconds"**. It works for their 10-second demo, but with a 15-minute interval the alarm would fire every minute, whenever the seconds match.
    *   We use `DS3231_A1_Hour` instead. The name is misleading, but it means **"match hours, minutes and seconds"**: the alarm fires once, at the exact time we computed, for any interval shorter than a day.
8.  **Go to Sleep:** We tell the ESP32 to wake up when `RTC_WAKEUP_PIN` (Pin 36) goes LOW, and call `esp_deep_sleep_start()`. If the alarm time is reached between `setAlarm1()` and the start of deep sleep, nothing is lost: the latched SQW line is already LOW, and the ESP32 wakes up immediately.

## Expected Output

When you run the code, you should see the ESP32 align on the 30-second grid, take a reading, and go back to sleep:

```text
--- Waking up from Deep Sleep ---
Wakeup by external signal using RTC_IO (RTC Alarm)
Data: 2026-07-22T15:47:00;29.33;33.06;997.36
Data saved to SD card.
Next reading scheduled for: 15:47:30
Entering Deep Sleep...

--- Waking up from Deep Sleep ---
Wakeup by external signal using RTC_IO (RTC Alarm)
Data: 2026-07-22T15:47:30;29.42;32.79;997.32
Data saved to SD card.
Next reading scheduled for: 15:48:00
Entering Deep Sleep...
```

*(Note: You will also see some ESP32 bootloader logs like `rst:0x5 (DEEPSLEEP_RESET)` printed between cycles. This is normal.)*

And if you pull the SD card and check `weather_data.csv`, you will see aligned data points:

```csv
timestamp;temperature;humidity;pressure
2026-07-22T15:47:00;29.33;33.06;997.36
2026-07-22T15:47:30;29.42;32.79;997.32
```

## Next Steps

The station now spends most of its time in deep sleep, keeps the BME280 asleep between measurements, and powers the SD card only when writing. According to our [estimates](02-hardware-modifications.qmd#power-budget-estimates), the remaining consumption in deep sleep is dominated by the modules around the ESP32, not by the ESP32 itself.

Next, we transmit this data to a server over Wi-Fi.
